bullet_groups.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: Opening with 'Because' delays the verb to the second clause, and 'strict access limits' is ambiguous (rate limits, permissions, query quotas?).
feedback.why_it_matters: On a skim the bullet reads as a database description; the retrieval design (precomputed category tree searched before the database, Redis for full records) is the part a retrieval-minded interviewer wants, and it's buried mid-sentence.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what kind of access limit (rate limit, quota, permission-gated).
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the action: 'Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree the Claude skill searches first ... because the 270K+ row table was [rate-limited/quota-limited]'.

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: Opens with a 20-word 'Because...' clause about table size and access limits, so the action ('precomputed popular workflows') arrives mid-line and the bullet ends on 'cut database queries' without telling me what the user of the tool gained.
feedback.why_it_matters: I could not restate why this mattered to a hiring manager without guessing; it reads as plumbing and I skipped it on the skim.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what problem 'strict access limits' caused for the tool (slow, blocked, rate-limited?) and how this bullet relates to the 65% speedup in the bullet above
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with what was built and for whom, then the constraint as a short reason; if it contributed to the 65% speedup, say so by merging or cross-referencing rather than adding a new number. e.g. 'Gave the Claude skill a fast first lookup: a precomputed category tree of popular workflows plus a Redis cache, since the 270K+ row PostgreSQL table had strict access limits'

feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
feedback.problem: The action arrives only after a long 'Because...' clause, and the sentence has no subject ('Because X, precomputed...'). 'strict access limits' is ambiguous: rate limits, query quotas, or permissions? 'category tree' and the 'with Redis caching...' tail are two separate designs stitched into one sentence.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader can't tell what constraint drove the design, so the design choice looks arbitrary. That makes it hard to defend under the question 'why not just add an index?'
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what kind of access limit (rate/quota/permission) forced the precompute
feedback.suggested_direction: Lead with the action and put the constraint after it, e.g. 'Precomputed popular workflows into a category tree the Claude skill searches first, because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL table had [kind of] limits, and cached full workflows in Redis'

bullet_groups.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often

feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp's candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often
feedback.problem: The bullet ends on 'tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often'. That is a prompt-only outcome with no stated evaluation: 'more often' has no comparison set, no trial count, and no definition of 'right grasp'. For an ML infra reader this is exactly the pattern that reads as hype, and it is the only bullet on the page under a 'Machine Learning Research' title.
feedback.why_it_matters: The interviewer's first question will be 'more often than what, measured how?'. If the bullet can't answer it, the real engineering (rendering grasp candidates into an image the VLM can choose from) gets discounted along with the vague ending.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: how 'right grasp' was judged (human label, sim success, real-robot trials), and against what baseline 'more often' was measured.
feedback.suggested_direction: Put the weight on the pipeline design (turning 3D grasp candidates into a visual multiple-choice for the VLM). If an evaluation set or success rate exists, name it; if not, replace 'more often' with the concrete method used to compare prompt variants, or end at the pipeline.

feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often
feedback.problem: Three unfamiliar names in a row ('AnyGrasp's candidate grasps', 'Open3D', 'vision-language model') before I know the goal, and the result 'more often' is unmeasured.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is one of the most ML-flavored roles on the page but it is the hardest to retell; 'more often' gives the reader nothing to repeat.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether any measured improvement in grasp selection exists; if not, keep it qualitative
feedback.suggested_direction: State the goal in plain words first (helping a vision-language model choose where a robot arm should grab an object), then the method; drop 'in Open3D' to Skills if space is needed.

feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often
feedback.problem: 'picks the right grasp more often' is the only result, and it is unquantified and unanchored. 'tuned prompts' is the thinnest kind of ML contribution and sits next to 'ICLR', which raises expectations.
feedback.why_it_matters: Pairing 'ICLR' with a vague 'more often' invites skepticism: an interviewer will ask 'how much more often, measured how?', and the page gives no footing.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: how grasp selection was evaluated (and the improvement, if it was measured)
feedback.suggested_direction: If a measured improvement exists, state it. If not, say how success was judged (e.g. on a held-out set of scenes) or soften 'aimed at ICLR' so the venue doesn't outrun the result.

bullet_groups.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio's class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio's class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency
feedback.problem: Ends on intent ('to reduce database load and latency') with no observed effect, and the 20,000+ visits number describes the product's traffic, not the caching work.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader skims the bold-free number, attributes 20K visits to the cache, then sees no cache result. It is the weakest bullet in an otherwise results-driven section and adds little for ML roles.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether hit rate, query count, or latency was measured after adding the cache.
feedback.suggested_direction: If a measured effect exists, end on it. If not, either name what was cached and why (which queries were hot) so the design choice carries the bullet, or cut it to give the RAG bullet more room.

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio’s class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency
feedback.problem: 'the studio's' is unclear (TerpLabs is never called a studio), and 'to reduce database load and latency' is intent with no outcome; the 20,000+ number describes the app, not this work.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader may credit the 20,000 visits to the caching work, or wonder what 'studio' refers to.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: 'studio' = TerpLabs?
feedback.suggested_direction: Introduce Tortuga first as the product ('Tortuga, TerpLabs' class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days'), then the caching; replace 'the studio's' with the company name.

feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio’s class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency
feedback.problem: The only number, 20,000+ visits, belongs to the product, not to the caching work, and the caching outcome is stated only as intent ('to reduce'). 'the studio' is undefined: the role header says TerpLabs, and the page never calls it a studio.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a borrowed metric. A skeptical reader sees a product-traffic number standing in for an engineering result, and the routine Redis-cache task becomes the bullet's whole content.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether caching had any observed effect; whether Amar built Tortuga itself or only the cache
feedback.suggested_direction: If Amar built Tortuga, lead with that and let the 20,000 visits be its result, with caching as the supporting detail. If he only added the cache, keep the traffic as context and say plainly that it was preventive. Replace 'the studio’s' with 'TerpLabs’'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Building capacity planning for Amazon Redshift maintenance like patching: Java logic that sets upper and lower bounds on reserved EC2 capacity to balance availability against cost, validated by backtesting

feedback.bullet: Building capacity planning for Amazon Redshift maintenance like patching: Java logic that sets upper and lower bounds on reserved EC2 capacity to balance availability against cost, validated by backtesting
feedback.problem: 'Java logic' after the colon is a noun phrase that hides what the logic is based on (forecasting, historical usage, rules), and 'maintenance like patching' reads awkwardly.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the top bullet on the page and the reader's first impression of the AWS role. 'Java logic' tells them the language but not the technique, so the bullet reads as generic.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what inputs the bounds are computed from (historical maintenance demand, forecasts, fleet size).
feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase as a full sentence that names the technique: 'Building Java logic that sets upper and lower bounds on reserved EC2 capacity for Redshift maintenance (e.g. patching) from [input], balancing availability against cost; validating it by backtesting'.

feedback.bullet: Building capacity planning for Amazon Redshift maintenance like patching: Java logic that sets upper and lower bounds on reserved EC2 capacity to balance availability against cost, validated by backtesting
feedback.problem: The colon after 'patching' turns the second half into a noun phrase ('Java logic that sets...') rather than a sentence, and 'Building capacity planning' is vague as a verb phrase. It is the top bullet under the biggest brand but is the least AI/ML-related item on the page.
feedback.why_it_matters: The first bullet a recruiter reads sets the frame; here it says 'cloud capacity', not 'AI/ML', for an AI/ML target. The stitched phrasing also reads less like the candidate talking.
feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase as one sentence with a real verb ('Writing Java logic that sets...'); keep it short since it is a 2-month-in role. Ordering is chronological so leave it, but keep it to one tight line-and-a-half.

feedback.bullet: Building capacity planning for Amazon Redshift maintenance like patching: Java logic that sets upper and lower bounds on reserved EC2 capacity to balance availability against cost, validated by backtesting
feedback.problem: The colon splits the bullet into a heading and a verbless fragment ('Java logic that sets...'), which nobody would say aloud. 'Building capacity planning' doesn't say whether he owns the whole capacity-planning effort or one component of it. 'maintenance like patching' reads as a typo for 'such as patching'.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the top bullet on the page and the biggest brand. A reader has to reparse it to see what Amar himself writes, and an interviewer will open with 'which part of this is yours?'
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: is the Java bounds logic the piece he owns, or the whole planner?
feedback.suggested_direction: Make it one sentence with a verb and a clear owner: what he is writing, what it decides, and why. Drop the colon. e.g. 'Writing the Java logic that sets upper and lower bounds on reserved EC2 capacity for Redshift maintenance such as patching, trading availability against cost, and checking it with backtests'

bullet_groups.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda

feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
feedback.problem: '34%' has no absolute baseline, and '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit (per day? per run? total corpus?).
feedback.why_it_matters: Latency claims are judged by the absolute number: 34% off 2 seconds and 34% off 20 minutes are very different engineering stories. Without the unit on 6,000+, the reader can't size the throughput.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: end-to-end latency before/after in seconds or minutes, and whether 6,000+ is per day or total.
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the mechanism (S3 staging hops replaced by Kinesis to Lambda), which is strong. Add the absolute latency and the time unit for the document count if known, e.g. 'from X to Y per document'.

feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
feedback.problem: 'S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda' is three AWS service names in a row; a non-engineer only gets 'changed how data moves'. Fine for an engineer, but 'staging hops' is jargon.
feedback.why_it_matters: Minor: the 34% lands, but the reason it got faster is opaque to a recruiter.
feedback.suggested_direction: Rephrase the method in plain words with the service names kept, e.g. 'by streaming documents through Kinesis to Lambda instead of writing each step to S3'.

feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
feedback.problem: '6,000+ scraped research documents' has no time unit: per day, per run, or total? The 34% has no absolute baseline (seconds? minutes?).
feedback.why_it_matters: The mechanism is clear and defensible, but scale is what makes a streaming change impressive, and without a unit the reader can't judge whether the volume justifies Kinesis.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: the time unit for 6,000+ documents and the latency baseline, if known
feedback.suggested_direction: Add the existing unit or baseline only if it exists. Otherwise leave as is. The mechanism phrase is good.

bullet_groups.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo's public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate

feedback.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo's public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate
feedback.problem: 'space-topic research tool' doesn't say what the tool does for the policy team, so the reader can't connect it to the classifier and pipeline bullets above.
feedback.why_it_matters: The handoff outcome is good production evidence, but without knowing what the tool is, the bullet reads as infrastructure for an unnamed thing.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tool lets policy staff do (search, filter, read ranked documents?) and whether it is the front end of the classifier pipeline.
feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'space-topic research tool' with a short functional description, and trim 'infrastructure-as-code' since CDK already implies it.

feedback.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo’s public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate
feedback.problem: Five tooling names (AWS CDK, infrastructure-as-code, GitHub Actions, CI/CD, Fargate) carry most of the bullet; 'space-topic research tool' does not tell me what the tool does for the policy team.
feedback.why_it_matters: The real win (the client's own engineers took it over) is buried at the end behind a tool list.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the research tool does for the policy team, in a few words
feedback.suggested_direction: Say what the tool does, then the handoff outcome; keep one or two infrastructure names and let Skills carry the rest.

feedback.bullet: Deployed a space-topic research tool for Amazon Leo’s public-policy team and set it up for handoff with AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD, so Leo engineers new to the project now maintain it on AWS Fargate
feedback.problem: 'space-topic research tool' is a noun stack that doesn't say what the tool does. The bullet then lists CDK, infrastructure-as-code, GitHub Actions, CI/CD and Fargate, so it reads mostly as deployment keywords. 'AWS Fargate' at the very end adds nothing to the handoff story.
feedback.why_it_matters: A non-engineer can't restate what was built. The real point, that other engineers took over maintenance, is buried under tool names.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the tool does for the policy team (search? summarize? track topics?)
feedback.suggested_direction: Say in a few plain words what the tool does. Keep CDK and CI/CD as the reason the handoff worked, and cut or move 'on AWS Fargate'.

bullet_groups.bullet: Cut LLM workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting one large Claude skill into smaller sub-skills that call Python tools for search and validation, and output quality held in repeated stress-test runs

feedback.bullet: Cut LLM workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting one large Claude skill into smaller sub-skills that call Python tools for search and validation, and output quality held in repeated stress-test runs
feedback.problem: 'Claude skill' and 'sub-skills' are vendor-specific terms that many ML/platform readers and most recruiters won't recognize as an agent/tool-use decomposition. The link between splitting and speed (smaller context per call? fewer tokens? parallel calls?) is also left implicit.
feedback.why_it_matters: The speedup is the headline AI result at a big-name company, but if the reader can't tell why splitting a skill made it faster, it reads as a prompt rearrangement rather than an engineering decision.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: why the split cut time (smaller prompts, deterministic Python doing work the model used to do, fewer retries).
feedback.suggested_direction: Gloss 'Claude skill' once in plain words (e.g. 'one large Claude agent prompt (skill)'), and name the reason the split was faster in a short clause. The quality phrase can stay as is.

feedback.bullet: Cut LLM workflow generation time 65% to under 15s by splitting one large Claude skill into smaller sub-skills that call Python tools for search and validation, and output quality held in repeated stress-test runs
feedback.problem: Three problems. (1) 'LLM workflow generation' is undefined here; the reader only learns in the third bullet that a 'workflow' is a test-data workflow. (2) The tail 'and output quality held in repeated stress-test runs' is a separate clause bolted on with 'and', with a new subject and no verb tying it to Amar. (3) The mechanism is unclear: the bullet never says why smaller sub-skills are faster (less context per call? parallel calls? fewer retries?).
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the strongest LLM-application claim for this target. A screener who doesn't know what's being generated can't value the 65%, and the obvious interview question, 'why did splitting make it faster?', isn't answered on the page.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what a 'workflow' is (test-data workflow?) and the reason the split reduced latency
feedback.suggested_direction: Name the output in plain words before the tech. Give the cause of the speedup in a few words. Turn the quality tail into a subordinate phrase, e.g. '...without losing output quality across repeated stress tests'

bullet_groups.bullet: Automated retraining for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance: on an EventBridge schedule a larger LLM grades its ratings, and fine-tuning runs only when the grades shift past a threshold

feedback.bullet: Automated retraining for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance: on an EventBridge schedule a larger LLM grades its ratings, and fine-tuning runs only when the grades shift past a threshold
feedback.problem: This is the best ML infra evidence on the page (scheduled LLM-as-judge evaluation gating fine-tuning), but 'the grades shift past a threshold' doesn't say what the shift is measured against, and the bullet has no outcome.
feedback.why_it_matters: An ML infra interviewer hires on evaluation-gated retraining, so they'll want to know whether the gate compares to a fixed baseline or a rolling window, and whether the judge was ever checked against human labels. Without that, the gate reads as a sketch rather than a tuned system.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the judge's grades are compared to (agreement rate with the classifier? drift from a prior window?) and what happened after it shipped (retrains triggered, fine-tunes avoided, stability).
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the structure. Swap 'the grades shift past a threshold' for the specific quantity being thresholded (e.g. 'agreement with the judge drops below a set level'), using only true details.

feedback.bullet: Automated retraining for a production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance: on an EventBridge schedule a larger LLM grades its ratings, and fine-tuning runs only when the grades shift past a threshold
feedback.problem: 'production Amazon Bedrock classifier that rates research documents by importance' is a long noun stack. Bedrock is a hosting service, not a model, so 'Bedrock classifier' invites the question 'what model is it?' The colon again splits the sentence into claim and explanation.
feedback.why_it_matters: This is the clearest ML-infrastructure bullet on the page (judge-triggered retraining), and the stacked phrasing hides it. An ML interviewer will probe what 'fine-tuning on Bedrock' means and what labels the judge produces.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which model the classifier is (an LLM hosted on Bedrock?)
feedback.suggested_direction: Split the noun stack into a sentence: say what the model does in plain words, then the trigger logic, with no colon. e.g. 'Automated retraining for a production LLM on Bedrock that rates research documents by importance, so a larger LLM grades its ratings on a schedule and fine-tuning runs only when those grades drift past a threshold'

bullet_groups.bullet: Building a RAG meal-suggestion feature for the official UMD app, in which GPT-4o mini writes suggestions from scraped recipes found by SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB, and internal testers rated 93% of meals satisfactory

feedback.bullet: Building a RAG meal-suggestion feature for the official UMD app, in which GPT-4o mini writes suggestions from scraped recipes found by SentenceBERT vector search in ChromaDB, and internal testers rated 93% of meals satisfactory
feedback.problem: 'for the official UMD app' is a large scope claim, but 'Building' plus 'internal testers' suggests it hasn't shipped, and the bullet doesn't say so. The middle chains GPT-4o mini, SentenceBERT and ChromaDB in one clause ('in which...found by...in...'). The bolded 93% has no tester count.
feedback.why_it_matters: A reader may assume it is live to UMD students. If it isn't, that is an awkward correction in an interview. The bold also draws the eye to the page's least-supported number.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether the feature is live in the UMD app or still in internal testing
feedback.suggested_direction: State the status plainly (e.g. 'in internal testing'). Shorten the retrieval chain to one plain phrase, such as 'retrieves similar recipes with embeddings', and keep model names in Skills. Consider unbolding 93%.

bullet_groups.bullet: Rebuilt the legacy tool developers use to create test-data workflows as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation, and 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it

feedback.bullet: Rebuilt the legacy tool developers use to create test-data workflows as a React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation, and 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it
feedback.problem: The middle is a tech run: React, TypeScript, Electron, React Flow and Jest, with React named twice. Only 'visual React Flow editor' explains a design choice. 'preferred it' leaves out the comparison (presumably over the legacy tool).
feedback.why_it_matters: This is a small cost. The stack list pads the line and dilutes the one interesting choice, the visual editor.
feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: preferred it over the legacy tool
feedback.suggested_direction: Keep 'visual editor' and the survey result. Move React/TypeScript/Electron/Jest to Skills or reduce them to one framing noun, e.g. '...as an Electron app with a visual drag-and-drop editor; 90% of 30+ surveyed developers preferred it to the old tool'

page_feedback.problem: The AI/ML story is spread across five roles and starts with a non-ML AWS capacity bullet; there is no single place where 'LLM applications / ML infrastructure engineer' jumps out in the first 7 seconds.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: On a skim I came away with 'cloud/backend person who uses LLMs', not 'ML infrastructure engineer'. The Bedrock retraining loop - the most ML-infra item - sits in the middle of the page.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep chronological order but make the first bullet of each role its most AI-relevant one; within the Amazon Leo role the retraining bullet is already first, which is good.

page_feedback.problem: The 'ML infrastructure' half of the intended profile rests on one bullet (judge-triggered retraining on Bedrock). The rest of the AI/ML evidence is LLM-API orchestration: Claude sub-skills, prompt tuning, and RAG with GPT-4o mini.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Applied-LLM teams will see a fit. ML-infrastructure teams will look for training, serving, or evaluation infrastructure and find mostly glue code around hosted models, so 'unusually strong systems engineer' comes across through the C++ project and AWS work rather than through the ML.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Bring forward the ML-infrastructure parts that already exist: the retraining trigger, the Kinesis inference pipeline, and the judge-based evaluation. Describe them as infrastructure decisions rather than LLM features.

page_feedback.problem: The strongest ML infra evidence (evaluation-gated retraining, Kinesis latency cut) sits in the third role, under a non-ML-sounding company heading 'UMD App Development Contracting'. The two roles above it open with capacity planning and an LLM-latency bullet.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A platform/ML infra screener skimming top-down sees AWS capacity planning first and has to reach mid-page to find the retraining loop that best matches the target.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep chronological order, but make sure the '(Client: Amazon Leo)' heading line and the retraining bullet are what the eye lands on: the retraining bullet is already first in its role. Consider tightening the AWS and Capital One bullets so that section starts higher on the page.

page_feedback.problem: Across the AI bullets, evaluation is mostly qualitative ('output quality held', 'picks the right grasp more often', '93% satisfactory'). Mechanisms are well named, but only the Bedrock bullet describes an evaluation loop, and none states an eval set or baseline.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: This reader's main filter is 'AI grounded in engineering, with an evaluation'. Its absence makes the AI work read more like LLM application building than ML infrastructure, which is a fit question for platform-team roles.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Without inventing metrics, describe the evaluation mechanism that existed (who or what judged, what it was compared against) in the bullets where it's known, starting with UMIACS and the Bedrock gate.

page_feedback.problem: 'Amazon Leo' and 'UMD App Development Contracting' are unexplained; a recruiter may not know Amazon Leo is an Amazon program, so the client brand does not land.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the role with the most ML-infra evidence, and the header is the most confusing one on the page.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Clarify in a few words what Amazon Leo is (e.g. a parenthetical on first mention) without adding new scope.

page_feedback.problem: The Skills section carries terms the bullets don't support: 'model fine-tuning' (only via Bedrock), 'OpenSearch', 'CloudWatch, X-Ray', 'Docker', 'uv', plus generic filler such as 'data structures and algorithms' and 'object-oriented design'. 'Open3D' sits under AI/ML.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: An interviewer may pick any listed item. The unsupported ones read as keyword padding, and the filler takes space from real skills.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Cut the generic items ('data structures and algorithms', 'object-oriented design'). Keep only the unsupported tools he can discuss in depth, and move Open3D out of AI/ML.

page_feedback.problem: 'UMD App Development Contracting (Client: Amazon Leo)' doesn't say what kind of organization this is (student club, university program, or his own contracting), so ownership and employer are ambiguous.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: These are some of the strongest bullets on the page. A reader who can't tell whether Amazon Leo was a real client under contract may discount them.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Clarify the organization type in the header in a few words, without adding scope.

page_feedback.problem: Three bullets use the colon/'Because' construction or stitch a second clause on with ', and' (AWS, the first Capital One bullet, Bedrock retraining, TerpLabs RAG). Read in a row, the pattern sounds generated rather than spoken.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The human-voice signal suffers: each bullet takes two passes to read, and a skeptical reader starts to wonder who wrote it.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Rewrite each as one subject-verb-object sentence with the result in a trailing clause. Avoid colons inside bullets.

page_feedback.problem: Several bullets use stacked tech names as the main content ('React and TypeScript Electron app with a visual React Flow editor and Jest-tested validation'; 'AWS CDK infrastructure-as-code and GitHub Actions CI/CD').
page_feedback.why_it_matters: These phrases are hard to say out loud and push human_voice and plain_language down; the Skills section already lists the tools.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep the one tool that explains the design choice in each bullet and leave the rest to Skills.

page_feedback.problem: 'Claude skill' / 'sub-skills' is product-specific jargon that many recruiters and engineers outside Anthropic's ecosystem won't recognize.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The Capital One LLM work is the domain headline, and its key noun may be read as 'Claude's ability' rather than a packaged agent capability.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: On first use, add a two- or three-word gloss (e.g. 'Claude skill (agent instructions plus tools)'), or describe it as an LLM agent with tools.

page_feedback.problem: Skills 'AI/ML' line mixes in 'Open3D' (a 3D geometry library) and 'prompt engineering', and uses 'Claude skills' as a skill term.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Minor: 'prompt engineering' as a listed skill weakens the systems-oriented framing for this reader, and Open3D fits better under a tools/libraries grouping.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Move Open3D out of the AI/ML line; consider dropping 'prompt engineering' since the bullets already show it in context.

page_feedback.problem: Bold is used only on numbers (65%, 90%, 34%, 93%, 50.9M) but not on the IEX 99,122 of 99,123 result, which is the most memorable number on the page.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: Bold drives the eye on a skim; the strongest proof point is unbolded while 50.9M (a volume, not a result) is bolded.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Consider moving the bold from '50.9M' to '99,122 of 99,123 fills'.
